summary: Reserved pool throughput degradation from client retry storm and sidecar I/O blocking
description: Issue summary: Argus Analytics' reserved GPU pool experienced a sustained throughput drop and elevated p99 latency starting 2026-03-12 09:10 UTC. Symptoms include queue growth for batched routes, frequent short-lived stream connections, and a wedge in autoscaler activity. Impact: customer observed ~60% throughput reduction for their critical inference routes and p99 latency increased from ~220ms to ~1.8s, causing timeouts downstream. Timeline: - 2026-03-12 09:05 UTC: first alerts from tenant-specific route (route: /v1/generate-argus). - 09:10: rapid increase in short-stream connections and 429s reported by customer SDK. - 09:15-10:30: autoscaler did not provision additional GPUs despite queue growth; several allocation attempts failed with node heartbeat delays. - 10:40: SRE discovered high NVMe write spikes on a subset of sidecars colocated with the reserved pool. Hypothesis: client-side retry loop produced a storm of short-lived streams which fragmented batchers and increased prefetch activity. Simultaneously a sidecar background snapshotter triggered heavy NVMe I/O, blocking scheduler heartbeats and preventing timely GPU allocations, compounding the throughput collapse.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Use a client that aggressively retries on 5xx/timeout with short stream sessions (open/close per request).
2) Send sustained high rate of short requests (~200 reqs/s) to a reserved pool route pinned to open-llama-13b.
3) Observe slot fragmentation (many short streams) and prefetch churn in serving-runtime metrics.
4) Trigger sidecar snapshotting (simulated heavy write) on the same nodes and watch for delayed node heartbeats and failed autoscaler allocations.
investigation_notes: Observed correlation between short-stream connection surge (client-side) and rise in prefetch eviction rate in serving-runtime.
Node-level telemetry: noisy NVMe write spikes on nodes hosting the customer's reserved pool sidecars concurrent with heartbeat delays.
Autoscaler logs show repeated allocation attempts that timed out waiting for kubelet/scheduler responses (node heartbeats delayed ~20-40s).
Reproduced locally by running a test harness that opens/closes streams per request and running snapshotter workload on same instance type — reproduced p99 spike and failed allocations.
Checked cross-tenant impact: other reserved pools on the same rack saw mild p50 increase but no full collapse; Argus pool was densest on affected nodes.
comments: Sofia Martinez (Support) [2026-03-12 09:30]: Reached out to Argus to request SDK logs and traffic profile. Asked for confirmation of SDK version and retry/backoff settings.

Argus (customer) [2026-03-12 09:45]: Confirmed running SDK v1.4.3 with default retry enabled; they reported seeing immediate 429s and client-side retries but said behavior started before their latest deploy.
Ravi Patel (SRE) [2026-03-12 10:05]: Scoped to serving nodes node-16..node-19. Noted high sidecar nvme I/O and autoscaler timeouts. Temporarily disabled snapshotter on node-17 as mitigation.

Sofia Martinez (Support) [2026-03-12 11:00]: Applied temporary customer workaround to disable aggressive client retries and increase connection pool on Argus SDK; customer reported immediate reduction in 429s and partial throughput recovery.

Ravi Patel (SRE) [2026-03-12 13:20]: Rolled out autoscaler sensitivity tweak to reduce heartbeat dependency window for allocation decisions in this reserved pool; further work planned to rate-limit short-lived streams at the API gateway.
resolution_notes: Workaround: instructed Argus to disable aggressive per-request retries and enable connection reuse in SDK (confirmed by customer at 2026-03-12 11:10 UTC). SRE disabled sidecar snapshotter on affected nodes and adjusted autoscaler heartbeat timeout to tolerate transient NVMe stalls. Result: throughput returned to ~85% of baseline and p99 dropped towards normal. Long-term: implementing API-gateway rate limiting for short-lived streams, adding sidecar snapshot randomization, and autoscaler improvements to detect NVMe-driven heartbeat pauses.
root_cause: Composite: (1) customer-facing SDK produced a retry storm of short-lived streaming connections that fragmented batchers and amplified prefetch churn; (2) a sidecar snapshotter job on the same nodes caused high NVMe I/O which delayed node heartbeats; together these prevented timely autoscaler allocations and led to sustained GPU shortage for the reserved pool.
follow_up_tasks: TASK-1: Build API-gateway heuristic to detect and throttle high-rate short-lived streams (owner: api team, ETA: 2w).
TASK-2: Add randomized snapshot schedule for sidecar snapshotter and cap nvme write IOPS (owner: infra team, ETA: 1w).
TASK-3: Improve autoscaler to consider node I/O health and not rely solely on heartbeat window for allocation decisions (owner: autoscale team, ETA: 3w).
TASK-4: Create a customer-facing best-practices note on client retries and connection reuse for dedicated pools (owner: developer-experience, ETA: 1w).
TASK-5: Attach alert that correlates sustained short-stream rate + nvme_iops spike and auto-create internal incident (owner: observability, ETA: 1w).
